metadata.narrative: Our town council is considering launching a free Saturday morning 5K in local parks where people can walk, jog, run, volunteer, or just come along, partly as a low-cost way to improve fitness and partly to reduce loneliness among older adults and people with mild mental health difficulties. What should we realistically expect such a program to do for physical activity, mental health, and social connection? How should we design it so it does not just attract already-active, affluent runners, and what tradeoffs or implementation risks should we keep in mind before we fund it?
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: The model your council is describing closely matches parkrun, the free, volunteer-led, weekly 5K held in local parks in more than twenty countries, so a large body of evidence on that program is directly applicable to expectations and design choices.

On physical activity, studies of new participants found that overall weekly activity increased after six months, though the effect faded somewhat by twelve months, and the gain was largest among people who were previously the least active, comparable in size to dedicated activity-promotion interventions.

Because the average completion time is roughly 28 and a half minutes, a single weekly attendance covers only about 19 to 38 percent of the UK's weekly physical-activity guideline depending on intensity, so the program should be framed as a meaningful but partial contribution to fitness.
Weight change has been modest but real, averaging about 1.1 percent loss over twelve months and higher, around 2.4 percent, among overweight and obese participants, without any dietary control.

On mental health, research on participants who identified as having mental health difficulties found consistent self-reported reductions in isolation, depression, anxiety and stress, alongside increased confidence and a sense of identity from being part of the "community."

Three recurring themes explain this: a sense of achievement from simply attending or improving, a feeling of connecting with others in a caring, non-competitive space, and a perception that the event is genuinely "for everyone," which participants described as more important to their wellbeing than the exercise itself.

Broader reviews find tension, depression, anger and stress fall from before to after events and that gains can persist a year later, though evidence is mixed: one Australian sample found wellbeing gains concentrated in the 55 to 64 age group, and another study found parkrun alone did not raise life satisfaction unless paired with increased running volume, so benefits should not be assumed to be automatic across all attendees.

On social connection specifically relevant to loneliness among older adults and people with mild mental health difficulties, participants felt "genuinely invested in and cared about" by other regulars, with improved self-esteem tied to being acknowledged and valued in a low-pressure, stigma-reducing environment.

Volunteering, not just running or walking, is central to this effect, since roles from marshal to run director let people who cannot or do not want to move at pace still participate fully, and physical-activity volunteering is independently associated with feeling worthwhile and improved life satisfaction.
However, the design details matter enormously for whether the program reaches people beyond already-active, affluent runners, since that is the most consistent criticism of mass participation events.

In the UK, parkrun is increasingly located in more disadvantaged urban areas, giving good geographic access, yet only about 13.1 percent of participants who have ever registered live in the most deprived areas, showing proximity alone does not close the participation gap.

Encouragingly, when people from deprived areas and previously inactive people do participate, they report the largest gains in physical activity and self-rated wellbeing of any group, meaning the people the council most wants to reach also stand to benefit the most if entry barriers can be lowered.

Participation is also skewed by gender and ethnicity: registration shows no gender bias but attendance does, with women less likely to attend regularly, and areas with higher densities of ethnic-minority residents show lower participation despite good geographic access, pointing to social rather than purely logistical barriers.

Qualitative work with women found the friendly atmosphere is the biggest draw, but the event can feel "cliquey" and intimidating to first-timers, and recorded times can read as competitive even though the point is a personal best, discouraging some beginners from returning.
Fear of judgement is identified as one of the single biggest general barriers to exercise participation, which supportive, non-competitive framing can reduce but not eliminate.

Disability inclusion also lags: only around 9 percent of participants report a disability or long-term health condition, and targeted efforts such as condition-specific accessibility guidance, outreach ambassadors, and volunteer sign-language and guide-runner roles have been needed to move that number.

Given this evidence, the council should treat inclusive design as ongoing work rather than a byproduct of making the event free, drawing on ground-up methods such as participatory action research with local volunteer organizers to surface site-specific barriers and tailor solutions rather than assuming one template works everywhere.

Concrete tactics with evidence behind them include recruiting peer champions for specific conditions, training volunteer guide runners for visually impaired participants, and considering beginner-only or women-only taster sessions modeled on approaches used in other mass-participation sports.

National policy analysis recommends "proportionate universalism," meaning the event should be open to everyone but should also actively target groups most in need, alongside removing practical fears such as disabled participants' concern that becoming more active could jeopardize disability benefits.
Several implementation risks and tradeoffs deserve attention before funding is committed.

Landowner and local-authority permission is not a formality: parkrun events have been suspended over safety complaints about blocked paths, and a parish council's attempt to charge a maintenance fee led to event cancellation until national government banned councils from charging for free fun runs, so path capacity, insurance, and no-fee commitments should be settled in advance.

Because the event depends entirely on unpaid volunteers for marshaling, timing, and results processing, sustainability hinges on recruiting and retaining enough volunteers to avoid burnout, a standing operational risk even though volunteering itself yields wellbeing benefits for participants.

Finally, the council should set realistic evaluation expectations: modest, fading physical-activity gains after a year, self-reported rather than clinically diagnosed mental-health improvement, and social-connection benefits strongest among people who return repeatedly and volunteer, not one-off attendees, so ongoing outreach and inclusive-design investment matter as much as the launch itself.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

On physical activity, studies of new participants found that overall weekly activity increased after six months, though the effect faded somewhat by twelve months, and the gain was largest among people who were previously the least active, comparable in size to dedicated activity-promotion interventions.

Because the average completion time is roughly 28 and a half minutes, a single weekly attendance covers only about 19 to 38 percent of the UK's weekly physical-activity guideline depending on intensity, so the program should be framed as a meaningful but partial contribution to fitness.
Weight change has been modest but real, averaging about 1.1 percent loss over twelve months and higher, around 2.4 percent, among overweight and obese participants, without any dietary control.

On mental health, research on participants who identified as having mental health difficulties found consistent self-reported reductions in isolation, depression, anxiety and stress, alongside increased confidence and a sense of identity from being part of the "community."

Three recurring themes explain this: a sense of achievement from simply attending or improving, a feeling of connecting with others in a caring, non-competitive space, and a perception that the event is genuinely "for everyone," which participants described as more important to their wellbeing than the exercise itself.

Broader reviews find tension, depression, anger and stress fall from before to after events and that gains can persist a year later, though evidence is mixed: one Australian sample found wellbeing gains concentrated in the 55 to 64 age group, and another study found parkrun alone did not raise life satisfaction unless paired with increased running volume, so benefits should not be assumed to be automatic across all attendees.

On social connection specifically relevant to loneliness among older adults and people with mild mental health difficulties, participants felt "genuinely invested in and cared about" by other regulars, with improved self-esteem tied to being acknowledged and valued in a low-pressure, stigma-reducing environment.

Volunteering, not just running or walking, is central to this effect, since roles from marshal to run director let people who cannot or do not want to move at pace still participate fully, and physical-activity volunteering is independently associated with feeling worthwhile and improved life satisfaction.
However, the design details matter enormously for whether the program reaches people beyond already-active, affluent runners, since that is the most consistent criticism of mass participation events.

In the UK, parkrun is increasingly located in more disadvantaged urban areas, giving good geographic access, yet only about 13.1 percent of participants who have ever registered live in the most deprived areas, showing proximity alone does not close the participation gap.

Encouragingly, when people from deprived areas and previously inactive people do participate, they report the largest gains in physical activity and self-rated wellbeing of any group, meaning the people the council most wants to reach also stand to benefit the most if entry barriers can be lowered.

Participation is also skewed by gender and ethnicity: registration shows no gender bias but attendance does, with women less likely to attend regularly, and areas with higher densities of ethnic-minority residents show lower participation despite good geographic access, pointing to social rather than purely logistical barriers.

Qualitative work with women found the friendly atmosphere is the biggest draw, but the event can feel "cliquey" and intimidating to first-timers, and recorded times can read as competitive even though the point is a personal best, discouraging some beginners from returning.
Fear of judgement is identified as one of the single biggest general barriers to exercise participation, which supportive, non-competitive framing can reduce but not eliminate.

Disability inclusion also lags: only around 9 percent of participants report a disability or long-term health condition, and targeted efforts such as condition-specific accessibility guidance, outreach ambassadors, and volunteer sign-language and guide-runner roles have been needed to move that number.

Given this evidence, the council should treat inclusive design as ongoing work rather than a byproduct of making the event free, drawing on ground-up methods such as participatory action research with local volunteer organizers to surface site-specific barriers and tailor solutions rather than assuming one template works everywhere.

Concrete tactics with evidence behind them include recruiting peer champions for specific conditions, training volunteer guide runners for visually impaired participants, and considering beginner-only or women-only taster sessions modeled on approaches used in other mass-participation sports.

National policy analysis recommends "proportionate universalism," meaning the event should be open to everyone but should also actively target groups most in need, alongside removing practical fears such as disabled participants' concern that becoming more active could jeopardize disability benefits.
Several implementation risks and tradeoffs deserve attention before funding is committed.

Landowner and local-authority permission is not a formality: parkrun events have been suspended over safety complaints about blocked paths, and a parish council's attempt to charge a maintenance fee led to event cancellation until national government banned councils from charging for free fun runs, so path capacity, insurance, and no-fee commitments should be settled in advance.

Because the event depends entirely on unpaid volunteers for marshaling, timing, and results processing, sustainability hinges on recruiting and retaining enough volunteers to avoid burnout, a standing operational risk even though volunteering itself yields wellbeing benefits for participants.

Finally, the council should set realistic evaluation expectations: modest, fading physical-activity gains after a year, self-reported rather than clinically diagnosed mental-health improvement, and social-connection benefits strongest among people who return repeatedly and volunteer, not one-off attendees, so ongoing outreach and inclusive-design investment matter as much as the launch itself.
